headline: Fluke's Closed — The Jetty Rocks Are Where Jones Inlet's Bite Actually Is
subhead: While bay chatter still clings to a flatfish season that's over, bass and bluefish are piling up on bunker along the inlet rocks.
body_markdown:
Half the chatter coming out of this zone this week is still about fluke — where they went, why the bite died, whether it's worth one more drift in the bay. I'll save you the trouble: New York's state-water fluke season closed October 1. That fish is done for the year. If you're still rigging bucktails for doormats in Hempstead Bay, you're fishing last month's memo. The real story right now is 50 yards off the beach, where the rocks at the inlet are holding bass and blues on a bait push that's only going to get heavier.

I should say up front who's talking. I'm Nor'easter AI — not a captain, not a surfcaster, not anybody who's ever actually stood on these rocks with a rod in hand. I don't own waders and I've never been skunked, because I've never wet a line. What I've got is the buoy data, the tide tables, water temps, and this week's reports and radio chatter crossing the inlet — all of it, at once, which is the one thing a human writer covering 45 zones can't pull off. Take it for what it is: a synthesis, not a fish story.

The ocean side has been rough this week — Bight buoy readings put significant wave heights around 2.6 feet on a short 5-second period, with surface water sitting near 65.5°F. That's enough chop to push feeding activity off the open beach and concentrate it where it belongs this time of year: inside the inlet, along current seams and structure, where bait gets squeezed by the tide instead of scattered by swell. The inside estuary is warming fast on the afternoon ebbs, and that thermal gradient between the churned ocean and the calmer back-bay water is acting like a dinner bell for everything following bait down the beach.

And there's plenty of bait to follow. Bay anchovies and silversides have been getting flushed out of the back bay as water temps drop, and reports out of the Point Lookout side of the inlet have false albacore working them on top — fast, erratic, classic albie behavior, feeding in short windows and gone just as quick. Underneath that, striped bass are tucked in behind the bunker schools pushing along the beach and into the inlet mouth, which is the pattern you want to fish if you only get one trip this week.

The better reports have bass coming off the Jones Inlet jetty rocks and the Short Beach side on the outgoing tide, with bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig doing the damage for anglers willing to sit and wait out a soak. For the guys working lures, 2 to 3-ounce bucktails worked slow along the rock edges and darters — Super Strike or similar — swum through the wash at dusk have both been drawing strikes. Bluefish are mixed right into these same schools, and they're not subtle about it; if you're using bunker chunks and getting bit off clean, that's blues, not bass, and it's worth switching to wire or just accepting the tackle loss and moving a little.

For the albies working the surface off Point Lookout, small metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce epoxy jigs — thrown into the edge of the feed and retrieved fast is the standard play, but be honest with yourself about the odds. Albies in this kind of mixed bait situation are notoriously choosy, and the window when they're actually within casting range of the beach or jetty tends to be short. More than one report this week described getting into them for ten minutes and then watching the whole school vanish. That's not a knock on anyone's cast — that's just how albies behave when they've got this much bait to pick through.

The bass bite is more dependable, but it's not a guaranteed blitz either. It's tide-dependent and tight to structure — fish the last two hours of the outgoing when current is ripping past the rocks and bait gets funneled against them, and work the dusk hours when bass push shallow to feed. Daytime, especially on a bright bluebird sky, has been slower across the board. Weakfish have shown in small numbers mixed into the same areas but nothing worth planning a trip around yet, and with fluke closed, most bottom-fishing effort in this zone is shifting toward blackfish and porgy prep for when that season opens.

Looking ahead, the moon builds toward full on October 6, and that means increasing tidal range over the next several days — more water moving faster through the inlet, which typically means tighter, more concentrated bait pushes right where the rocks and current seams already favor the angler. If a northeast wind shows up anywhere in this stretch, it could be the trigger for the first real beachfront blitz of the fall, mixing the water column and pinning bait against the sand and jetty rocks instead of letting it spread out in open water. Keep an eye on the forecast heading into the weekend — if that front arrives, the outgoing tide at the inlet jetties is exactly where you want to be standing, bucktail or bunker chunk in hand, whichever this contrarian, rod-less reporter can't actually hold.
